The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

items.quote: Nevertheless , linear relationships between the adsorbed and gas-phase entropies persist for acidic $ ^ { 25 } $ and siliceous frameworks , $ ^ { 10 } $ suggesting that geometric descriptors may be suitable in further developing empirical correlations . The ideal gas entropy can be rigorously derived using statistical mechanics and depends on the degrees of freedom of the molecule. The greatest contributions to the gas-phase entropy are typically from the translational and rotational modes, which under isothermal conditions primarily depend on the system volume and principle moments of inertia of the molecule, respectively. Considering that adsorption limits the accessible volume and potentially hinders the rotational freedom of a molecule, it is conceivable that the entropy of adsorption may be predicted by using geometric arguments. For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration and the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{26} $ De Moor et al. $ ^{27} $ used ab initio simulations to show that the adsorption entropies for n-alkanes within acidic zeolites are linearly correlated with their carbon number. Janda et al. $ ^{28} $ have studied the topological effects of protonic zeolites on the thermodynamics of n-alkane adsorption using Monte Carlo simulations. The conclusions of their work showed that for unidimensional zeolites without cages, the ratio of the minimum to maximum channel diameters positively correlate with the entropy and enthalpy of adsorption. In particular, the enthalpy and entropy of adsorption become less negative for adsorption within channels which are oval shaped and are most negative for circular-shaped channels. They showed that the presence/absence of framework cages also impacts the thermodynamics of adsorption, suggesting that the alkanes exhibit more rotational freedom in cages vs channels. Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman $ ^{25} $ compiled experimentally determined adsorption entropies for alkanes adsorbed in nine aluminosilicate zeolites. They showed that the entropic loss upon adsorption could be linearly correlated with the molecule's gas-phase translational and rotational entropies and that the occupiable volume of a zeolite is a “universal” descriptor in predicting such losses. In a separate study, $ ^{10} $ we have qualitatively reproduced the trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman's work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions. items.quote: The molecular weight is a fundamental physical quantity with a presence in the statistical mechanical expression of the translational entropy for an ideal gas, as well as in the hindered/free translator entropy approximation for adsorbates within protonic zeolites. $ ^{[11,13-16]} $ Likewise, the molecular weight is also related to the number of heavy atoms (non-hydrogen) of the molecule, which has been shown to linearly correlate with the adsorption entropy of alkanes within protonic zeolites. $ ^{[27]} $ Under standard conditions, the translational entropy is the most significant contribution toward the absolute entropy of a molecule and predictably experiences the most significant loss upon adsorption. The rotational moments of inertia make for excellent descriptors toward distinguishing among spherical, linear, and nonlinear adsorbates. Namely, molecules represented by a single sphere exhibit no rotational inertia, while linear and nonlinear molecules rotate about two and three axes, respectively. Collectively, the principle moments provide additional information about the shape of the molecule. For example, the ratio of the principle moments (i.e., $ I_1/I_3 $ and $ I_2/I_3 $) describes the molecule as being “rod-like”, “sphere-like”, “disc-like”, or “envelope-like”.⁵¹,⁵² More complicated expressions can also be derived and presumably learned by a NN model, such as the “molecular eccentricity”,⁵³ “inertial shape factor”,⁵² and “sphericity index”,⁵⁴ each of which provide additional information about the shape of the molecule. The rotational freedom of a molecule is generally the second largest contributor to the standard ideal-gas entropy of the adsorbate, and the principle moments of inertia are explicitly present in the rotational entropy equation. The principle moments are also found within the hindered/free rotor approximation for alkanes within protonic zeolites and organic molecules on two-dimensional catalytic surfaces.¹¹,⁵⁵,⁵⁶

The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

Considering that adsorption limits the accessible volume and potentially hinders the rotational freedom of a molecule, it is conceivable that the entropy of adsorption may be predicted by using geometric arguments. For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration and the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{26} $ De Moor et al. $ ^{27} $ used ab initio simulations to show that the adsorption entropies for n-alkanes within acidic zeolites are linearly correlated with their carbon number. As shown in the next section , one can introduce physically intuitive arguments into more complicated models of entropy than that presented above . 4.3. Empirical Model of Entropy Based on Adsorbent Identity. While the linear entropy scaling in Figures 1 and 3 is quite successful for the TraPPE-based adsorption systems, it is ultimately an oversimplified correlation. We seek a physics-based structure—topology—entropy relationship that is generic and applicable across molecule classes and zeolites. As a first step to this end, motivated by the arguments in refs 13 and 27, we considered a simple linear model wherein each contributor to the entropy is affected differently. However, it has been argued that the translational contribution to the adsorbate entropy (for alkanes) is relatively uniform across frameworks, with the emphasis being on the disparate rotational contributions. $ ^{13,58} $ For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration with the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{58} $ Therefore, we consider a model where $ s_{ads}^{\infty} $ is composed of (1) two-third translational entropy (equivalent to the loss of one-third of the gas-phase translational entropy) and (2) a fraction of the gas-phase rotational entropy. As mentioned previously, the vibrational entropy is assumed to be unaffected by adsorption or confinement. We propose the simplest model consistent with the proposition that the adsorbed-phase entropy is composed of the translational and rotational entropies and all of the vibrational entropy of the gas state.
